kurz: The green in vegetables is chlorophyll. Heat and acid turn it into an olive-brown pigment. Short cooking keeps it bright.
bild_im_kopf: Like a light bulb on a timer: in the first minutes the green even glows brighter, then it gets duller with every minute.
was_passiert: In the first minutes in hot water, green vegetables even turn brighter, because air escapes from the tissue. As cooking goes on, [[saeure|acids]] leak out of the cells and turn chlorophyll into an olive-brown pigment. [[natron|Baking soda]] in the water neutralises the acid and keeps the green, but destroys vitamins and makes the vegetables mushy.
warum_wichtig: Explains why beans in a stew turn grey and why restaurants [[blanchieren|blanch]] vegetables and plunge them into iced water.
faustregeln: Cook briefly in plenty of rapidly boiling salted water.
Plunge into iced water straight away so it does not [[nachgaren|carry on cooking]].
Add lemon or vinegar only just before serving.
No baking soda in the cooking water: it keeps the green, but makes the vegetables mushy and destroys vitamins.

praxis.text: Beans, peas, broccoli: blanch, refresh, and mix with sauce only when serving.

mythos.behauptung: Cooking with the lid on keeps vegetables green.
mythos.richtig: Rather the opposite: without a lid, volatile acids can escape. But short cooking times and plenty of water matter more.
